title: FEHB and Medicare Part B: A Retiree's Guide

payload.title: FEHB and Medicare Part B: A Retiree's Guide
payload.excerpt: Federal retirees can keep FEHB, add Medicare Part B, or suspend FEHB. This guide compares costs and coordination of benefits to help you decide.
payload.author: David Haass
payload.seoTitle: FEHB and Medicare Part B: A Retiree's Guide
payload.seoDescription: Should you combine FEHB and Medicare Part B? Compare costs, coordination of benefits, and incentives to decide what's best for federal retirees.

structuredSections.text: FEHB and Medicare Part B: What You're Really Deciding

structuredSections.content: There is no single right answer for every federal retiree weighing [Medicare Part B](/faqs/medicare-part-b-explained-premiums-deductibles-coverage-and-enrollment-in-2026/) against their Federal Employees Health Benefits (FEHB) plan. The better choice depends on your [health needs](/faqs/what-is-medicare/), your budget, and how much [financial risk](/faqs/medicare-cost-sharing/) you are comfortable carrying. One thing worth knowing upfront: FEHB coverage does not end when you become eligible for Medicare. You keep your FEHB plan unless you choose to drop or suspend it.

That means you are really choosing among three paths: keep FEHB only, keep FEHB and add Part B for extra coverage, or suspend FEHB and rely mainly on Medicare. Each option carries different costs and tradeoffs, which the rest of this guide breaks down.

structuredSections.text: How FEHB and Medicare Part B Work Together

structuredSections.content: When you have both FEHB and Medicare, the two coordinate benefits rather than duplicate them. For most retirees, Medicare becomes the primary payer and FEHB pays second, covering costs Medicare does not pick up, such as remaining deductibles, coinsurance, or copays. This coordination can lower what you pay out of pocket compared to having FEHB alone.

Part B specifically helps cover outpatient care, doctor visits, and preventive services. If your FEHB plan leaves you responsible for a percentage of these costs, Part B can absorb much of that gap, since Medicare pays its share first and FEHB often picks up what remains.

structuredSections.text: Why Some FEHB Plans Reward You for Having Both

structuredSections.content: Some FEHB carriers offer incentives specifically for members who also enroll in [Medicare Part B](/faqs/medicare-part-b-explained-premiums-deductibles-coverage-and-enrollment-in-2026/). These can include reduced out-of-pocket maximums, waived deductibles, or lower copays for hospital stays and outpatient visits. The incentives vary significantly by carrier and plan year.

Because these programs are not standard across all FEHB plans, check your specific plan brochure for a section on Medicare coordination or [Medicare Part B](/faqs/medicare-part-b-explained-premiums-deductibles-coverage-and-enrollment-in-2026/) incentives. This is usually listed under a heading addressing members who have Medicare as a secondary payer.

structuredSections.text: Comparing the Real Costs: Premiums, IRMAA, and Out-of-Pocket Spending

structuredSections.content: Adding Part B means paying its monthly premium on top of your existing FEHB premium. The standard Part B premium in 2026 is $202.90 per month, though this amount rises if your income is above certain thresholds.

structuredSections.calloutText: Retirees with higher reported income pay an Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount (IRMAA) on top of the standard Part B premium. In 2026, surcharges push the total monthly Part B premium as high as $689.90 for the highest income bracket.

structuredSections.content: Consider a moderate healthcare user comparing FEHB alone against FEHB plus Part B. With FEHB only, this retiree might pay $0 extra in Part B premiums but absorb more coinsurance and copays throughout the year, especially for specialist visits or outpatient procedures. Adding Part B means paying roughly $2,435 a year in Part B premiums at the standard rate, but potentially saving a comparable or greater amount in reduced coinsurance, depending on how much care they use and whether their FEHB plan offers a dual-enrollment incentive.

structuredSections.text: When Part B's Added Premium Pays for Itself

structuredSections.content: Retirees who see specialists frequently, manage chronic conditions, or anticipate outpatient procedures tend to benefit most from adding Part B. The reduced coinsurance and deductible exposure can offset the monthly premium over a full year, particularly if your FEHB plan offers a financial incentive for Medicare enrollees.

IRMAA is based on your reported income from two years prior, so your 2026 Part B premium is determined by your 2024 tax return. According to the [Social Security Administration's IRMAA guidance](https://www.ssa.gov/), this amount is reassessed annually and can change as your income changes.

IRMAA is added on top of the standard Part B premium, not charged instead of it. A retiree filing jointly with income between $218,000 and $274,000 would pay $284.10 per month total for Part B in 2026, combining the standard premium and the surcharge.

Before you decide, ask your FEHB plan directly whether it offers a reduced deductible or lower out-of-pocket maximum for members enrolled in [Medicare Part B](/faqs/medicare-part-b-explained-premiums-deductibles-coverage-and-enrollment-in-2026/). This single detail can shift the math significantly, and it is not always obvious from a quick read of your plan brochure.

structuredSections.text: Will Your Doctors and Prescriptions Still Be Covered?

structuredSections.content: Most FEHB plans already provide nationwide access to a broad network of providers, so adding Part B typically does not expand which doctors you can see. Where dual coverage matters more is if you travel frequently, split time between two residences, or plan to relocate, since having Medicare alongside FEHB can simplify billing with providers who are used to working with Medicare's claims process.

On prescriptions, check whether your current FEHB drug coverage meets Medicare's creditable coverage standard. Most FEHB plans do meet this standard, which means you generally will not face a late enrollment penalty if you decide to add Medicare Part D later. Confirm this detail in your plan's annual notice of creditable coverage rather than assuming it applies.

structuredSections.text: Avoiding Common Mistakes and Missed Deadlines

structuredSections.content: Federal retirees typically have a Special Enrollment Period tied to their retirement date and Medicare eligibility, during which they can enroll in Part B without facing a late enrollment penalty. Missing this window can result in a permanent premium increase, since Medicare's [late enrollment penalty for Part B](https://www.medicare.gov/basics/costs/medicare-costs) adds 10% to your premium for each 12-month period you were eligible but did not enroll.

structuredSections.calloutText: If you drop FEHB to rely on Medicare and later change your mind, re-enrolling in FEHB is not automatically guaranteed. Confirm the specific rules with your HR benefits office before making an irreversible decision.

structuredSections.content: Before finalizing your decision, ask your agency's HR benefits office or the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) these questions: What happens to my FEHB premium if I suspend coverage and later want it back? Does my plan offer a Medicare incentive program? What is my exact Special Enrollment Period deadline based on my retirement date?

structuredSections.text: How to Decide What's Right for Your Situation

items: Health status: Do you see specialists often or manage ongoing conditions that generate regular medical bills?
Budget flexibility: Can you comfortably absorb an added monthly Part B premium, including any IRMAA surcharge?
Travel habits: Do you split time between locations or travel often enough that simplified claims processing would help?

structuredSections.content: Rather than focusing only on the monthly premium, compare your total estimated annual cost under each option, including premiums, deductibles, and expected coinsurance based on your typical healthcare use. A licensed Medicare agent familiar with FEHB coordination can walk through this comparison with you at your own pace, without pressure to enroll before you are ready.

structuredSections.text: FAQ: FEHB and Medicare Part B Questions Federal Retirees Ask

faqs.question: Do I have to decide about Part B right when I retire?
faqs.answer: You generally have a Special Enrollment Period tied to your retirement date and Medicare eligibility, giving you time to research before enrolling. You do not need to decide the day you retire, but the window does have a deadline, so confirm your specific dates with your HR benefits office to avoid a late enrollment penalty.

faqs.question: Will someone try to pressure me into adding Part B?
faqs.answer: A licensed Medicare agent can explain your FEHB and Part B options clearly without pushing you toward a decision. The choice should be based on your health needs and budget, not a sales quota. If you ever feel rushed, it is reasonable to ask for time to review the comparison on your own.

faqs.question: Can I just read my FEHB plan brochure and figure this out myself?
faqs.answer: Your plan brochure contains useful details about coordination with Medicare, but the language can be dense and hard to compare against other options. Reading it is a good starting point; pairing that research with a professional review can help confirm you understand how the numbers apply to your specific situation.

faqs.question: What if I add Part B and later decide it wasn't worth it?
faqs.answer: You can typically drop Part B later, though doing so may affect future enrollment timing and could involve a late enrollment penalty if you want to re-enroll. Since income and health needs change, it is worth reviewing your costs annually rather than assuming your initial decision is permanent.

structuredSections.text: Your Next Step Toward a Confident Decision

structuredSections.content: Choosing between FEHB alone, FEHB with Part B, or a shift toward relying on Medicare comes down to weighing the added premium cost against the reduced risk of unpredictable out-of-pocket spending. There is no deadline pressure to decide today, but your enrollment window does have a real end date.

Before that window closes, consider requesting a personalized cost comparison based on your FEHB plan, income, and typical healthcare use. Having clear numbers in front of you, rather than general assumptions, makes it easier to choose coverage you will feel settled with.

keyTakeaways: FEHB coverage does not end at Medicare eligibility; you choose to keep it, add Part B, or suspend FEHB
When combined, Medicare typically becomes primary payer and FEHB pays second, reducing out-of-pocket costs
Some FEHB carriers offer incentives like waived deductibles or lower copays for members enrolled in Part B
The standard 2026 Part B premium is $202.90 per month, rising to $689.90 for high earners due to IRMAA surcharges
Retirees with frequent specialist visits or chronic conditions often benefit most from adding Part B
